---
title: "Session 5: Generative network models"
subtitle: "Compared to what? Building and using random networks"
date: today
---

## Goals

- build a random network by hand and understand what "random" means for a network,
- know what random networks look like: Poisson degrees, no hubs, a giant component, short paths,
- contrast random and scale-free networks: hubs, degree heterogeneity, small and ultra-small worlds,
- use random networks as baselines in practice: pick a null model, simulate, locate the observed value,
- see what random networks teach us about power: hubs, brokers, exit options and vulnerability.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(igraph)

set.seed(2027)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
```

## 1. The question: is this a lot?

```{r}
g <- make_graph("Zachary")   # swap in the course dataset here
transitivity(g)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Think first"}
Is a transitivity of about 0.26 high or low? You cannot answer without asking: compared to what?
:::

Every network statistic needs a comparison. A random network is that comparison: what the network would look like if ties formed without any structure, preference or mechanism. Whatever the observed network has beyond that is what needs explaining.

## 2. Building a random network by hand

A random network (Erdős–Rényi) has one rule: **every possible tie exists with the same probability p, independently of all others.** Think of a coin flip for every pair of nodes.

We build one ourselves, without igraph's generator, to see that there is nothing more to it.

```{r}
n <- 20
p <- 0.15

pairs <- combn(n, 2)                 # all 190 possible pairs
coin  <- runif(ncol(pairs)) < p      # one coin flip per pair: TRUE with probability p
edges <- pairs[, coin]

g_hand <- make_graph(as.vector(edges), n = n, directed = FALSE)

plot(g_hand, vertex.size = 10, vertex.label = NA, vertex.color = "grey30")
c(possible_ties = ncol(pairs), drawn_ties = ecount(g_hand), expected = p * ncol(pairs))
```

Run the chunk again: a different network every time, but always around 0.15 × 190 ≈ 28 ties.

igraph has two versions of the same idea:

```{r}
g_gnp <- sample_gnp(n, p)        # fix the probability p: the number of ties varies
g_gnm <- sample_gnm(n, m = 28)   # fix the number of ties m: placed at random
c(gnp = ecount(g_gnp), gnm = ecount(g_gnm))
```

To build a baseline for an observed network, we usually fix the number of nodes and ties to match it, so `sample_gnm(vcount(g), ecount(g))`.

## 3. What random networks look like

Because every tie is a coin flip, a random network is very predictable. Four properties follow directly, and we can check each by simulation.

### Degrees: everyone is average

Each node has n − 1 coin flips, so its expected degree is ⟨k⟩ = p(n − 1). Some nodes get a few more, some a few less, but the degrees cluster tightly around the mean. The distribution is (approximately) **Poisson**.

```{r}
n <- 1000
k_mean <- 10
g_er <- sample_gnp(n, k_mean / (n - 1))

tibble(degree = degree(g_er)) |>
  count(degree) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(degree, share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(y = dpois(degree, k_mean))) +   # the Poisson prediction
  labs(x = "Degree k", y = "Share of nodes with degree k",
       subtitle = "Bars: simulated random network. Line: Poisson with mean 10.")

c(mean = mean(degree(g_er)), max = max(degree(g_er)))
```

The key consequence: **no hubs.** With a mean of 10 among 1,000 nodes, the best-connected node has only around 20 ties. A node with 100 ties essentially never occurs.

### Clustering: equal to density

In a random network, two of my partners are tied with probability p, just like any other pair. So clustering ≈ density.

```{r}
c(transitivity = transitivity(g_er), density = edge_density(g_er))
```

This is why we compared clustering with density in the previous sessions: density is what clustering would be in a random network.

### The giant component

Start with no ties and raise the mean degree slowly. At first the network is a dust of small fragments. Then, at ⟨k⟩ = 1, one component suddenly grows to span a large share of all nodes. This sharp change is called a **phase transition**.

```{r}
giant <- tibble(k = seq(0, 4, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(share_largest = map_dbl(k, \(k) {
    x <- sample_gnp(1000, k / 999)
    max(components(x)$csize) / 1000
  }))

ggplot(giant, aes(k, share_largest)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Mean degree ⟨k⟩", y = "Share of nodes in the largest component")
```

One partner on average is enough to connect most of the system. Two or three partners on average connect almost everyone.

### Short paths: the small world

In a random network with mean degree ⟨k⟩, a node reaches about ⟨k⟩ others in one step, ⟨k⟩² in two steps, ⟨k⟩³ in three. Reach grows exponentially, so the number of steps needed to reach everyone grows only with the logarithm of N:

$$
\langle d \rangle \approx \frac{\ln N}{\ln \langle k \rangle}
$$

```{r}
small_world <- tibble(N = c(100, 300, 1000, 3000)) |>
  mutate(avg_path  = map_dbl(N, \(N) mean_distance(sample_gnm(N, N * 2))),   # ⟨k⟩ = 4
         predicted = log(N) / log(4))

small_world
```

Thirty times more nodes add only about two or three steps. This is the **small-world** property, and random networks already have it.

## 4. Random versus scale-free networks

Real networks often look different from random ones in one striking way: they have hubs. A **scale-free** network is one whose degree distribution follows a power law, $p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}$: many nodes with few ties, and a few hubs with very many. Preferential attachment, "the rich get richer", is one mechanism that produces it.

We build both networks with the same size and the same mean degree, so the only difference is how ties are distributed.

```{r}
n <- 2000
g_sf <- sample_pa(n, m = 2, directed = FALSE)   # preferential attachment, ⟨k⟩ ≈ 4
g_rn <- sample_gnm(n, ecount(g_sf))             # random, same N and same number of ties

both <- bind_rows(
  tibble(network = "random",     degree = degree(g_rn)),
  tibble(network = "scale-free", degree = degree(g_sf))
)

both |>
  group_by(network) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(degree), median = median(degree), max = max(degree))
```

Same mean, but the maximum differs by a factor of five or more.

### Two views of the degree distribution

On ordinary axes the random network forms a bump and the scale-free network a steep L-shape. On log–log axes the difference becomes clear: the random network falls off a cliff, while the scale-free network declines along an almost straight line.

```{r}
dist <- both |>
  count(network, degree) |>
  group_by(network) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

ggplot(dist, aes(degree, share, shape = network)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(random = 1, `scale-free` = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Degree k", y = "Share of nodes", shape = NULL, subtitle = "Linear axes")

ggplot(dist, aes(degree, share, shape = network)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(random = 1, `scale-free` = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Degree k (log)", y = "Share of nodes (log)", shape = NULL, subtitle = "Log–log axes")
```

### Measuring how dominant the hubs are: ⟨k⟩ and ⟨k²⟩

The table in Barabási (2016, Table 4.1) describes networks with ⟨k⟩ and ⟨k²⟩. The mean ⟨k⟩ tells you how many ties a typical node has. The mean of the squared degrees, ⟨k²⟩, tells you how unequal they are, because squaring makes large degrees count much more: a hub with 100 ties contributes 10,000.

In a random network ⟨k²⟩ is close to ⟨k⟩ + ⟨k⟩², so for ⟨k⟩ = 4 about 20. With hubs it is much larger. The ratio ⟨k²⟩ / ⟨k⟩ is a quick heterogeneity index.

```{r}
heterogeneity <- function(x) {
  k <- degree(x)
  c(N = vcount(x), L = ecount(x),
    k_mean = mean(k), k2_mean = mean(k^2), ratio = mean(k^2) / mean(k))
}

rbind(random     = heterogeneity(g_rn),
      scale_free = heterogeneity(g_sf),
      observed   = heterogeneity(g)) |>
  round(1)
```

This gives you the same columns as Table 4.1 for your own network.

### Is my network scale-free?

`fit_power_law()` estimates the exponent γ and tests whether a power law fits the tail of the distribution.

```{r}
fit <- fit_power_law(degree(g_sf), implementation = "plfit")
c(gamma = fit$alpha, xmin = fit$xmin, p_value = fit$KS.p)
```

A p-value above 0.05 means a power law cannot be rejected, not that it is proven.

::: {.callout-warning title="Most networks are not strictly scale-free"}
A heavy tail is common; a clean power law is not. Broido and Clauset (2019, Nature Communications) tested almost 1,000 networks and found strong evidence for a power law in only a small minority. IR networks are also small (about 200 states), which leaves too few nodes in the tail to estimate γ reliably. In practice, ask the more useful question: are there hubs, and how dominant are they? ⟨k²⟩ / ⟨k⟩ and the maximum degree answer that without requiring a power law.
:::

### Small world versus ultra-small world

Hubs act as shortcuts: many paths run through them. So distances in a scale-free network are even shorter than in a random network of the same size and mean degree. Barabási calls this an **ultra-small world**.

```{r}
distances_by_size <- tibble(N = c(100, 300, 1000, 3000)) |>
  mutate(
    random     = map_dbl(N, \(N) { s <- sample_pa(N, m = 2, directed = FALSE)
                                   mean_distance(sample_gnm(N, ecount(s))) }),
    scale_free = map_dbl(N, \(N) mean_distance(sample_pa(N, m = 2, directed = FALSE)))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-N, names_to = "network", values_to = "avg_path")

ggplot(distances_by_size, aes(N, avg_path, linetype = network)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of nodes N (log)", y = "Average path length", linetype = NULL)
```

Both grow slowly, but the scale-free network stays consistently shorter.

### Between order and randomness: the small-world model

Random networks have short paths but almost no clustering. Real networks often have both. Watts and Strogatz showed that a few random shortcuts are enough: start with a regular ring where everyone is tied to their nearest neighbours (high clustering, long paths), then rewire each tie with probability p.

```{r}
ws <- tibble(p = 10^seq(-4, 0, length.out = 15)) |>
  mutate(stats = map(p, \(p) {
    x <- sample_smallworld(dim = 1, size = 500, nei = 5, p = p)
    tibble(clustering = transitivity(x), avg_path = mean_distance(x))
  })) |>
  unnest(stats)

ws_base <- ws |> slice(1)

ws |>
  mutate(clustering = clustering / ws_base$clustering,
         avg_path   = avg_path / ws_base$avg_path) |>
  pivot_longer(c(clustering, avg_path), names_to = "measure", values_to = "relative") |>
  ggplot(aes(p, relative, linetype = measure)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Rewiring probability p (log)", y = "Relative to the ordered ring (p = 0.0001)",
       linetype = NULL)
```

Around p = 0.01, path length has already collapsed while clustering is still almost intact. A handful of long-range ties, such as a few cross-regional agreements, turns a world of regional clusters into a small world.

## 5. Using random networks as baselines in practice

This is the main practical use of random networks. The recipe has four steps:

1. **Pick the statistic** you want to judge, for example transitivity.
2. **Pick the null model**: decide what the random networks should keep fixed.
3. **Simulate** many networks from the null model and compute the statistic in each.
4. **Locate the observed value** in that distribution.

### Step 2 matters most: what is held fixed?

| Null model | Keeps fixed | Randomises | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Random graph, `sample_gnm()` | number of nodes and ties | everything else | is this more than chance, given the density? |
| Configuration model, `rewire(keeping_degseq())` | every node's degree | who is tied to whom | is this more than the degree distribution alone produces? |
| Attribute permutation, `sample()` on an attribute | the whole network | which node has which attribute | do ties follow the attribute more than chance? |

The configuration model is the stricter and usually more useful baseline. Many patterns, including clustering and short paths, arise partly because some nodes are very active. Holding degrees fixed removes that explanation.

One consequence: anything a null model keeps fixed cannot look surprising. Under the configuration model, maximum degree is identical in every simulation. That is not a finding; it is the design.

### A reusable comparison function

```{r}
network_stats <- function(x) {
  b <- betweenness(x)
  c(transitivity      = transitivity(x),
    avg_path          = mean_distance(x),
    degree_assort     = assortativity_degree(x),
    max_degree        = max(degree(x)),
    top3_betweenness  = sum(sort(b, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]) / sum(b))
}

null_models <- list(
  random_graph  = \(x) sample_gnm(vcount(x), ecount(x)),
  configuration = \(x) rewire(x, with = keeping_degseq(niter = ecount(x) * 10))
)

compare_to_null <- function(x, null_fun, reps = 500) {
  sims <- map(1:reps, \(i) as_tibble_row(network_stats(null_fun(x)))) |> list_rbind()
  obs  <- network_stats(x)

  sims |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "statistic", values_to = "simulated") |>
    group_by(statistic) |>
    summarise(null_mean = mean(simulated),
              null_low  = quantile(simulated, 0.025),
              null_high = quantile(simulated, 0.975),
              null_sd   = sd(simulated),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(observed = obs[statistic],
           z        = (observed - null_mean) / null_sd) |>
    select(statistic, observed, null_mean, null_low, null_high, z)
}
```

`top3_betweenness` is the share of all brokerage held by the three most central brokers: a simple measure of how concentrated control over flows is.

### Run it

```{r}
results <- imap(null_models, \(f, name) compare_to_null(g, f) |> mutate(null_model = name)) |>
  list_rbind()

results |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) round(v, 2)))
```

Read each row as: the observed value, the range in which 95% of random networks fall, and how many standard deviations the observed value lies from the random mean (z). Values of |z| above about 2 mean the observed network is clearly unlike the null model on that statistic.

All statistics on one common axis, z-scores:

```{r}
results |>
  filter(is.finite(z)) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, statistic, shape = null_model)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -2, xmax = 2, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(random_graph = 1, configuration = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Distance from the null model (z-score). Grey band: within ±2",
       y = NULL, shape = "Null model")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Think first"}
Which statistics are surprising against the random graph but not against the configuration model? What does that tell you: is the pattern a feature of how ties are arranged, or only of how many ties each node has?
:::

### Attribute permutation: testing homophily

For homophily the network stays fixed and only the attribute is shuffled. We use the karate club with its known split into two factions.

```{r}
data("karate", package = "igraphdata")   # install.packages("igraphdata") if needed
karate <- upgrade_graph(karate)

obs_assort <- assortativity_nominal(karate, V(karate)$Faction, directed = FALSE)

perm_assort <- replicate(1000,
  assortativity_nominal(karate, sample(V(karate)$Faction), directed = FALSE))

tibble(assortativity = perm_assort) |>
  ggplot(aes(assortativity)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_assort) +
  labs(x = "Faction assortativity with shuffled faction labels (1,000 permutations)",
       y = "Number of permutations", subtitle = "Vertical line: observed")

mean(perm_assort >= obs_assort)   # share of shuffles at least as homophilous as observed
```

The share in the last line is a permutation p-value. With real IR data the same code tests, for example, whether democracies tie to democracies more than a random assignment of regime types would produce.

## 6. What random networks teach us about power

Hafner-Burton, Kahler and Montgomery (2009) describe three sources of network power: **access** (high degree), **brokerage** (sitting between others) and **exit options** (having alternatives). Random networks show what each looks like when it is absent.

- **High degree.** In a random network, degrees are Poisson: nobody has many more partners than anyone else. Hubs are a sign that the network is not random, and hubs are where access power concentrates.
- **Brokerage.** In a random network, shortest paths are spread over many nodes. Concentrated betweenness, as in `top3_betweenness` above, means a few actors control flows between others.
- **Exit options.** In a random network, every node's partners are interchangeable and most have alternatives. When ties run through a few hubs, the spokes have no exit: losing the hub means losing access.

### Robustness: random failure versus targeted attack

The sharpest way to see this is to remove nodes and watch the network fall apart. We compare removing nodes at random with removing the best-connected nodes first.

```{r}
largest_share_after_removal <- function(x, fraction, how) {
  k <- round(fraction * vcount(x))
  if (k == 0) return(1)
  drop <- if (how == "targeted") order(degree(x), decreasing = TRUE)[1:k] else sample(vcount(x), k)
  max(components(delete_vertices(x, drop))$csize) / vcount(x)
}

robustness <- expand_grid(
  network  = c("random", "scale-free"),
  how      = c("random failure", "targeted attack"),
  fraction = seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.025)
) |>
  mutate(share_largest = pmap_dbl(
    list(network, how, fraction),
    \(network, how, fraction) {
      x <- if (network == "random") g_rn else g_sf
      largest_share_after_removal(x, fraction, if (how == "targeted attack") "targeted" else "random")
    }))

ggplot(robustness, aes(fraction, share_largest, linetype = how)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ network) +   # same axes in both panels
  labs(x = "Share of nodes removed", y = "Share of nodes still in the largest component",
       linetype = NULL)
```

Read the two panels together:

- The **random** network degrades the same way whether nodes are removed at random or deliberately. There are no hubs to target.
- The **scale-free** network survives random failure well, since most removed nodes are unimportant spokes. But removing the few hubs breaks it apart quickly.

This is the network logic behind weaponized interdependence (Farrell and Newman 2019). Global finance and supply chains are not random networks: they run through a few hubs such as SWIFT or dollar clearing. That makes them robust to everyday disruptions and highly vulnerable to whoever controls the hubs, whether by attack or by denial of access.

::: {.callout-note title="Think first"}
Which IR networks would you expect to look random, and which scale-free? Consider embassy networks, arms trade, investment treaties and submarine internet cables. For which ones does it matter most who the hubs are?
:::
